chunks.title: What the Internet of Things is
chunks.content: The Internet of Things (IoT) is a network of physical objects, called things, that have sensors, software and network connectivity so they can collect data and exchange it with other devices and systems over the internet. Each thing needs a unique identity, such as an IP address or a device ID, so that it can be found and addressed. Things sense their environment, for example temperature, motion or light, and some can also act on it through actuators such as motors, valves or switches. Key characteristics of IoT are connectivity, sensing, unique identity, heterogeneity (devices from many vendors with different hardware and protocols), very large scale (billions of devices) and dynamic change, because devices join, leave, move or sleep to save energy. Many IoT devices are constrained: they have little memory, low processing power and run on batteries.

chunks.title: Applications of IoT
chunks.content: IoT is used in many sectors. In smart homes, connected lights, thermostats, door locks and cameras can be monitored and controlled from a phone, and rules can automate them, such as turning off lights when nobody is in a room. In agriculture, soil moisture sensors tell an irrigation system when to water crops, which saves water. In healthcare, wearable devices track heart rate or blood glucose and can alert doctors remotely. In industry, sensors on machines measure vibration and temperature to predict failures before they happen, which is called predictive maintenance. In smart cities, IoT supports smart parking, street lights that dim when roads are empty, and air quality monitoring.

chunks.title: Challenges of IoT
chunks.content: IoT also brings challenges. Security is a major one: many devices ship with default passwords and rarely get software updates, so attackers can take them over, for example to build a botnet. Privacy is another, because sensors in homes and wearables collect personal data about people's habits and health. Interoperability is hard because devices from different vendors use different protocols and data formats, so they cannot always work together; standards and gateways help. Energy is limited for battery-powered devices, so they must use low-power hardware and radios and sleep most of the time. Scalability matters because a system may have to manage millions of devices and handle large volumes of data.

chunks.title: Components of an IoT system
chunks.content: A typical IoT system has several components. Sensors measure physical quantities such as temperature, humidity or motion, and actuators change the physical world, for example by switching a relay or turning a motor. The sensors and actuators are attached to an IoT node (device), usually built around a microcontroller with a radio. A gateway connects local devices to the internet and can translate between protocols, for example from Zigbee or Bluetooth to Wi-Fi or Ethernet, and can filter or aggregate data. The network carries the data, and a cloud or server platform stores and analyses it. Finally, an application or user interface, such as a mobile app or dashboard, lets people see the data and send commands. In home automation, a motion sensor in a room sends an event through a hub (gateway) to the cloud, and a rule turns on the light.

chunks.title: Layered IoT architectures
chunks.content: IoT architectures are often described in layers. The basic three-layer architecture has a perception layer, a network layer and an application layer. The perception layer (also called the sensing or device layer) contains sensors and actuators that collect data from the physical world. The network layer transmits that data to other devices and servers using technologies such as Wi-Fi, cellular networks, Zigbee or LoRa. The application layer delivers services to users, such as a smart home app or a smart city service. A five-layer architecture adds a processing layer (middleware) between the network and application layers to store, analyse and process large amounts of data, and a business layer on top that manages the whole system, including business models and user privacy.

chunks.title: Communication models and design goals
chunks.content: IoT devices communicate in four common models. In the device-to-device model, devices talk directly to each other, for example a light switch and a bulb using Bluetooth or Zigbee. In the device-to-cloud model, a device connects directly to a cloud service over the internet, for example through Wi-Fi. In the device-to-gateway model, devices connect to a local gateway, such as a smartphone or hub, which forwards data to the cloud. In the back-end data-sharing model, data collected in one cloud service is shared with other authorised services so they can combine and analyse it. Design goals for IoT systems include low power consumption, low cost per device, scalability, reliability, security and privacy by design, and interoperability between devices from different vendors.

chunks.title: MQTT basics
chunks.content: MQTT (Message Queuing Telemetry Transport) is a lightweight messaging protocol designed for constrained devices and unreliable networks. It uses a publish/subscribe model: clients do not send messages directly to each other but to a central server called a broker. A client that sends data publishes a message to a topic, a text string such as home/livingroom/temperature, and the broker forwards the message to every client that has subscribed to that topic. Topics are hierarchical, with levels separated by slashes. Subscribers can use wildcards: the plus sign (+) matches exactly one level, so home/+/temperature matches home/kitchen/temperature, and the hash sign (#) matches all remaining levels and must be the last character, so home/# matches every topic under home. MQTT runs over TCP; the default port is 1883, and 8883 is used for MQTT over TLS.

chunks.title: MQTT quality of service and session features
chunks.content: MQTT offers three Quality of Service (QoS) levels for delivering a message. QoS 0 means at most once: the message is sent once without acknowledgement, so it may be lost. QoS 1 means at least once: the sender keeps the message until it receives a PUBACK, so the message arrives but may be duplicated. QoS 2 means exactly once: a four-step handshake (PUBLISH, PUBREC, PUBREL, PUBCOMP) makes sure the message arrives once, at the cost of more overhead. A retained message is stored by the broker for its topic and sent immediately to new subscribers, so they get the last known value. The Last Will and Testament is a message the client registers when it connects; the broker publishes it if the client disconnects unexpectedly. The keep-alive interval tells the broker how long the client may stay silent; the client sends PINGREQ packets to show it is still connected.

chunks.title: CoAP
chunks.content: CoAP (Constrained Application Protocol) is a web transfer protocol for constrained devices and networks, standardised by the IETF in RFC 7252. Like HTTP it follows the REST style: resources are identified by URIs and accessed with the methods GET, POST, PUT and DELETE, and responses use codes similar to HTTP, such as 2.05 Content or 4.04 Not Found. Unlike HTTP, CoAP runs over UDP, by default on port 5683, and uses a compact 4-byte fixed header to save bandwidth and energy. Because UDP is unreliable, CoAP has its own message types: Confirmable (CON) messages must be acknowledged with an Acknowledgement (ACK) and are retransmitted if no ACK arrives; Non-confirmable (NON) messages are not acknowledged; a Reset (RST) message indicates that a received message could not be processed. With the Observe option, a client can register interest in a resource and the server sends notifications whenever it changes.

chunks.title: Classification of sensors
chunks.content: A sensor detects a physical quantity, called the measurand, and converts it into a signal that a circuit can use, usually an electrical voltage, current, resistance or capacitance. Sensors are classified in several ways. By measurand: temperature, pressure, acceleration, displacement, proximity, light or humidity sensors. By the need for an external power source: a self-generating sensor produces its own electrical signal from the energy it measures, for example a thermocouple, which generates a small voltage from heat, a solar cell or a piezoelectric sensor; an externally excited sensor needs an excitation or power source to produce its output, for example a thermistor, an RTD or a strain gauge, whose resistance can only be read by passing a current through it. The labels active and passive are used for these two groups in opposite ways: many Indian engineering texts (NPTEL / IIT) call self-generating sensors active and excited sensors passive, while some other books use the reverse, so it is clearer to describe the group than to rely on the label. By output: an analog sensor gives a continuous signal, while a digital sensor already gives a digital value, for example over a serial bus. Sensors can also be contact (touching the object) or non-contact (for example infrared or ultrasonic).

chunks.title: Case studies: accelerometer, proximity and temperature sensors
chunks.content: A capacitive MEMS accelerometer contains a tiny proof mass held by springs. When the device accelerates, the mass moves relative to the frame, and because the mass forms a movable plate between fixed plates, the capacitance between the plates changes; often one capacitance increases while the other decreases. The readout measures this change, which is proportional to the acceleration. Accelerometers are used in phones, wearables and vibration monitoring. Displacement and proximity sensors detect position or the presence of a nearby object: capacitive sensors detect a change in capacitance, inductive sensors detect metal objects through a change in inductance, and ultrasonic sensors measure the time of flight of an echo, so distance = speed of sound x time / 2. Temperature sensors include the thermistor, whose resistance changes strongly with temperature (an NTC thermistor's resistance falls as temperature rises), giving high sensitivity but a non-linear response over a limited range; the RTD, usually platinum, whose resistance rises almost linearly and which is accurate and stable; the thermocouple, two different metals joined at a junction that produce a small voltage of tens of microvolts per degree, which works over a very wide range up to more than 1000 degC and, with a small junction, responds quickly; and IC temperature sensors that give a linear output such as 10 mV per degC.

chunks.title: Sensor characteristics
chunks.content: Sensor characteristics describe and compare sensors. Range is the span between the smallest and largest value the sensor can measure. Sensitivity is the change in output per unit change in input, the slope of the response, for example 10 mV per degC. Specificity (selectivity) means the sensor responds only to the intended quantity and not to others, such as a gas sensor that also reacts to humidity. Resolution is the smallest change in input that produces a detectable change in output. Accuracy is how close a reading is to the true value, while precision is how close repeated readings of the same input are to each other; a sensor can be precise but not accurate. Threshold is the smallest input, starting from zero, that produces a detectable output. Linearity describes how closely the output follows a straight line against the input; the largest deviation from that line is the non-linearity error. Stability is the ability to give the same output for the same input over time; slow change is called drift. Hysteresis means the output for the same input depends on whether the input was increasing or decreasing. Response time is how long the sensor takes to reach its final output, often to 63% or 90% of it, after a sudden change in input.

chunks.title: The sensor readout chain
chunks.content: Sensor readout is the electronics that turns a sensor's output into numbers a microcontroller can use. Many sensor signals are small analog signals, millivolts or even microvolts as from a thermocouple, or a change in resistance or capacitance. A typical readout chain has a front end that turns the sensor change into a voltage (for example by passing an excitation current through a resistive sensor), an amplifier, usually built with an operational amplifier (opamp), that scales the voltage to the input range of the analog-to-digital converter (ADC), the ADC itself, which samples and quantizes the voltage into a digital code, and finally the microcontroller that processes the codes. Amplification before the ADC matters: if a 50 mV signal is fed to an ADC with a 5 V range, it uses only about 1% of the range, so only a few output codes change and the effective resolution is poor.

chunks.title: Analog-to-digital conversion
chunks.content: An ADC converts an analog voltage into a digital code in two steps: sampling and quantization. Sampling takes the value of the signal at regular instants; the sampling rate is the number of samples per second. To capture a signal correctly, the sampling rate must be more than twice the highest frequency in the signal (the Nyquist criterion); if it is lower, fast changes are missed and the signal appears at a wrong, lower frequency, which is called aliasing. An N-bit ADC has 2^N possible output codes spread over its full-scale input range, set by the reference voltage Vref. The size of one step, the least significant bit (LSB), is Vref / 2^N. For example, an 8-bit ADC with Vref = 2.048 V has 256 codes and an LSB of 8 mV. The ADC's resolution in the measured quantity is the LSB divided by the sensor's sensitivity.

chunks.title: Quantization and readout design choices
chunks.content: Quantization maps each sampled value to the nearest of the ADC's discrete levels, so a continuous input becomes a staircase. The difference between the true value and the quantized value is the quantization error; with rounding to the nearest level it is at most half an LSB, and it behaves like a small added noise. Using more bits makes the LSB smaller and the resolution finer, but the ADC usually costs more, uses more power, converts more slowly and produces more data. Readout design involves a few choices: choose the amplifier gain so that the largest sensor signal comes close to, but does not exceed, the ADC full-scale range, because a signal above full scale saturates (clips) at the maximum code; choose the number of bits so that the LSB, expressed in the measured quantity, is smaller than the resolution the application needs; and choose a sampling rate comfortably above twice the signal's highest frequency, but not much higher than needed, to save power and data.

chunks.title: Readout non-idealities: ideal and real opamps
chunks.content: Readout circuits are designed as if the opamp were ideal: infinite input resistance, so it draws no current from the sensor; zero output resistance; infinite open-loop gain; infinite bandwidth; and zero offset, so a zero input gives a zero output. Real opamps only approximate these properties. Each difference, called a non-ideality, adds an error to the reading. The error is usually small, but it becomes important when the sensor signal is tiny, when the gain is large, when the sensor has a high output resistance or when the signal changes quickly. Designers therefore check the opamp's datasheet limits against the needs of the sensor and the application.

chunks.title: Opamp input resistance and loading
chunks.content: A sensor can be modelled as a voltage source Vs with an output (source) resistance Rs. When it is connected to an amplifier with input resistance Rin, current flows through Rs and part of the voltage is lost across it: Rs and Rin form a voltage divider, so the amplifier sees only Vs x Rin / (Rs + Rin). This is the loading effect. If Rin is much larger than Rs, the loss is negligible; for example Rs = 1 kOhm and Rin = 1 MOhm keep 99.9% of the voltage. If Rin is comparable to Rs, the reading is noticeably too low. The fix is to make the input resistance much larger than the source resistance, typically by placing a buffer (a voltage follower, an opamp with gain 1 and very high input resistance) between the sensor and the rest of the circuit, or by choosing an opamp with a very high input resistance, such as one with CMOS or FET inputs.

chunks.title: Other opamp non-idealities
chunks.content: Input offset voltage is a small DC voltage, typically microvolts to a few millivolts, that acts as if it were added to the input: the output is not exactly zero when the input is zero. The amplifier multiplies the offset by its gain, so a 1 mV offset with a gain of 100 gives a 0.1 V error at the output. Input bias current is the small current that flows into the opamp's input pins; flowing through the sensor's source resistance, it creates an extra error voltage, which is significant for high-resistance sensors. Because the open-loop gain is finite, the closed-loop gain of an amplifier is slightly lower than the value set by its resistors. The bandwidth is limited: the gain-bandwidth product is roughly constant, so the higher the gain, the lower the frequency at which the gain starts to fall. The slew rate is the maximum rate at which the output voltage can change; faster, large signals are distorted. Finally, the output cannot swing beyond the supply voltages, so a too-large signal saturates.

chunks.title: Why data analysis for IoT
chunks.content: IoT systems produce very large amounts of data: many sensors report readings continuously, often every few seconds, and the data comes in many forms, such as temperatures, vibrations, images and logs. Raw readings are of little use until they are analysed. Data analysis turns them into information and decisions. Typical goals are monitoring (showing the current state of a system on a dashboard), prediction (for example predicting a machine failure before it happens, called predictive maintenance, or forecasting energy demand), anomaly detection (finding readings that do not fit the normal pattern, such as a sudden temperature spike that may mean a fault or an attack) and automation (letting the system act by itself, such as switching irrigation on when the soil is predicted to be dry). Because the rules behind the data are often unknown or too complex to write by hand, IoT data analysis often uses machine learning, which learns a model from the data itself.

chunks.title: Components and feasibility of learning
chunks.content: Learning from data can be described with a few components. There is an unknown target function f that maps an input x (for example the vibration readings of a motor) to an output y (for example whether the motor will fail soon). We do not know f, but we have a data set of examples (x, y) collected in the past. A learning algorithm searches a hypothesis set, the family of candidate models it is allowed to choose from (for example all straight lines), and picks the final hypothesis g that fits the data best, hoping that g is close to f. Learning is feasible, in a probabilistic sense, when the data are representative of the situations where the model will be used and there are enough examples: then a model that does well on the training data is likely to do well on new data too. The error on the training data is the in-sample error; the error on new, unseen data is the out-of-sample error. These terms (target function, hypothesis set, final hypothesis, in-sample and out-of-sample error) come from the widely used Learning From Data framework; other courses may simply call the final hypothesis the trained model. A model that is too complex can fit the training data almost perfectly, including its noise, yet perform badly on new data; this is called overfitting.

chunks.title: Types of learning and data-driven techniques
chunks.content: There are three main types of learning. In supervised learning, every training example has the correct answer (a label): if the output is a number it is regression, for example predicting tomorrow's energy use, and if it is a category it is classification, for example faulty or normal. In unsupervised learning, the data has no labels and the algorithm looks for structure by itself, for example clustering similar devices. In reinforcement learning, an agent learns by trial and error from rewards, for example a thermostat that learns a schedule from comfort feedback. A data-driven project follows a pipeline: collect the data; clean it by handling missing values and removing or correcting outliers caused by faulty sensors; choose or compute features, such as the average vibration over a minute; split the data into a training set to fit the model and a test set, kept aside, to check how well it works on unseen data; train the model; and evaluate it. In Python, NumPy handles arrays of numbers, pandas handles tables of data such as sensor logs, scikit-learn provides models such as linear regression and k-means, and matplotlib draws plots.

chunks.title: Linear regression
chunks.content: Linear regression models the relationship between an input x and a numeric output y with a straight line, y = w0 + w1 x, where w0 is the intercept (the value of y when x is 0) and w1 is the slope (how much y changes when x increases by 1). The line is fitted by least squares: the weights are chosen to minimise the mean squared error (MSE), the average of the squared differences between the predicted and the actual values. For example, if the fitted line is y = 1.5 + 0.2 x, an input of x = 10 gives a prediction of 1.5 + 0.2 x 10 = 3.5. The model is evaluated on test data, for example with the MSE: a smaller MSE means better predictions. A fitted line should only be trusted within the range of inputs it was trained on; predicting far outside that range is extrapolation and can be badly wrong, because the relationship may not stay linear.

chunks.title: Time-series data and models
chunks.content: A time series is a sequence of measurements taken in time order, usually at regular intervals, such as a temperature reading every hour. A time series is often described by three components: the trend, a long-term increase or decrease; seasonality, a pattern that repeats with a fixed period, such as a daily or weekly cycle; and noise, the random variation that is left. A moving average, the mean of the last few values, smooths out noise so the trend is easier to see. An autoregressive (AR) model predicts the next value as a weighted sum of previous values; to capture a daily cycle in hourly data, it can also use the value from 24 hours earlier. Because the order of the data matters, a time series must not be shuffled before splitting: the model is trained on the earlier part and tested on the later part, so that it is never tested on the past using knowledge of the future.

chunks.title: Clustering
chunks.content: Clustering is an unsupervised technique that groups data points so that points in the same group (cluster) are similar and points in different groups are different. The most common algorithm is k-means. First choose the number of clusters k and pick k starting centres (centroids). Then repeat two steps: assign every point to its nearest centroid, and move each centroid to the mean of the points assigned to it. Stop when the assignments no longer change. The value of k is often chosen with the elbow method: plot the total distance of points to their centroids for several values of k and pick the k where adding more clusters stops giving a large improvement. Because k-means uses distances, features with large numeric ranges would dominate, so the features are usually scaled (standardised) first. In IoT, clustering can group households by their energy-use profiles or sensors by their behaviour, and a reading that is far from every centroid can be flagged as an anomaly.

questions.content: What does each IoT device need so that it can be found and addressed on a network?
options: A unique identity such as an IP address or device ID
A large colour touch screen for local user input
A permanent wired connection to the electricity grid
A full desktop operating system such as Windows
questions.explanation: Each thing needs a unique identity, such as an IP address or device ID, so that it can be found and addressed.

questions.content: Which term describes IoT devices that have little memory, low processing power and run on batteries?
questions.explanation: Devices with little memory, low processing power and battery power are called constrained devices.

questions.content: Which component lets an IoT device act on the physical world, for example by opening a valve?
questions.explanation: Actuators such as motors, valves or switches act on the physical world; sensors only measure it.

questions.content: What is predictive maintenance in industrial IoT?
options: Replacing every machine on a fixed yearly schedule
Repairing machines only after they have broken down
Buying spare machines in case one of them fails
Using machine sensor data to predict failures early
questions.explanation: Sensors measure vibration and temperature so failures can be predicted before they happen.

questions.content: In smart agriculture, which sensor tells an irrigation system when crops need water?
questions.explanation: Soil moisture sensors tell the irrigation system when to water crops, which saves water.

questions.content: What does interoperability mean for IoT devices?
options: Devices can run for years on a single battery
Devices from different vendors can work together
Devices can encrypt every message that they send
Devices can be installed without any network
questions.explanation: Interoperability is the ability of devices from different vendors, protocols and data formats to work together.

questions.content: Why are many IoT devices easy for attackers to take over?
options: They always use the newest and strongest encryption
They are never connected to the public internet at all
They often keep default passwords and rarely get updates
They are protected by a powerful firewall in the cloud
questions.explanation: Many devices ship with default passwords and rarely get software updates, so attackers can take them over.

questions.content: A smart thermostat measures room temperature and switches the heater on when the room gets cold. Which two IoT capabilities does it use?
questions.explanation: It senses the temperature (sensor) and acts on the heater (actuator).

questions.content: A smart-city network has thousands of sensors from different vendors; some sleep to save energy and new ones are added every month. Which pair of IoT characteristics does this show?
questions.explanation: Devices from many vendors show heterogeneity; devices that sleep, join and leave show dynamic change.

questions.content: A hospital wants to watch a patient's heart rate at home and alert the doctor if it becomes dangerous. Which IoT application area is this?
questions.explanation: Wearable devices that track heart rate and alert doctors remotely are a healthcare (remote monitoring) use.

questions.content: A city wants its street lights to use less energy late at night when roads are empty. Which IoT solution fits best?
options: Replacing all street lights with brighter bulbs
Switching every street light off for the whole night
Lights with motion sensors that dim when nobody is near
Asking residents to report broken lights by email
questions.explanation: Smart street lights dim when roads are empty, saving energy without leaving roads dark.

questions.content: A company buys smart locks from vendor A and a hub from vendor B, but the hub cannot control the locks because they use different protocols. Which IoT challenge is this?
questions.explanation: Devices from different vendors using different protocols that cannot work together is an interoperability problem.

questions.content: A fitness band records sleep times and location all day and uploads them to the cloud. Which concern does this raise most directly?
questions.explanation: Wearables collect personal data about people's habits and health, which is a privacy concern.

questions.content: Why do battery-powered IoT sensors usually sleep most of the time and wake up only to send data?
options: To get more processing power from the CPU
To save energy so the battery lasts longer
To make the radio signal travel much further
To store more readings in their small memory
questions.explanation: Energy is limited for battery-powered devices, so they sleep most of the time to save it.

questions.content: Explain what the Internet of Things is and what an object needs in order to become part of it.

rubric.text: Things exchange data over a network (any one of: collect data, send data, share data, exchange data).
What an object needs (both needed: sensors; network connectivity).
Each thing has a unique identity

questions.explanation: Model answer: The Internet of Things is a network of physical things that collect and exchange data over the internet. An object needs sensors, software and network connectivity. It also needs a unique identity, such as an IP address.

questions.content: Describe how IoT is used in healthcare and in industry, and give the benefit of each.

rubric.text: Healthcare use of IoT (any one of: wearables track heart rate or blood glucose, doctors are alerted remotely).
Industry: sensors on machines measure vibration or temperature
Industry benefit (any one of: failures predicted before they happen, fewer breakdowns, less downtime).

questions.explanation: Model answer: In healthcare, wearable devices track a patient's heart rate or blood glucose and alert doctors remotely when something is wrong. In industry, sensors on machines measure vibration and temperature, so the company can predict failures before they happen and repair the machine in time.

questions.content: Explain why security and privacy are serious problems for IoT devices used in homes.

rubric.text: Devices are easy to break into (any one of: default passwords, weak passwords, rarely updated).
Attackers can take the devices over (any one of: hijack, control the device, use it in a botnet).
Sensors collect personal data about people (any one of: habits, health, daily life).

questions.explanation: Model answer: Many home IoT devices ship with default passwords and rarely get software updates, so attackers can take them over and use them in a botnet. Privacy is also at risk, because cameras, sensors and wearables collect personal data about people's habits and health.

questions.content: IoT devices and systems are often described as constrained, heterogeneous and dynamic. Explain what each of these three characteristics means.

rubric.text: Constrained: devices have limited resources (any one of: little memory, low processing power, battery power).
Heterogeneous: devices differ from each other (any one of: many vendors, different hardware, different protocols).
Dynamic: the set of devices keeps changing (any one of: devices join, leave, move, go offline).

questions.explanation: Model answer: Constrained means that many devices have little memory and low processing power and run on batteries. Heterogeneous means that the devices come from many vendors with different hardware and protocols. Dynamic means that devices join, leave or move all the time, so the system keeps changing.

questions.content: A farm wants to use less water for irrigation. Describe an IoT solution: which device measures the field, which device acts on the water supply, and what rule the system follows.

rubric.text: Soil moisture sensors measure the field
An actuator such as a valve or pump controls the water
Rule: water only when the soil is dry or below a threshold
Benefit: less water is used

questions.explanation: Model answer: Soil moisture sensors are placed in the fields to measure how wet the soil is. A valve on the water pipe is the actuator that the system opens or closes. The rule is to open the valve only when the soil is dry, so the farm saves water.

questions.content: A city plans to install 100,000 IoT sensors from several vendors, most of them running on batteries. For each of these three challenges — security, interoperability and energy — suggest one concrete way to handle it. Also explain why energy matters so much for this project.

rubric.text: Security: one concrete protection (any one of: unique or strong passwords, regular updates, encryption).
Interoperability: require open standards or use gateways that translate protocols
Energy: one way to save power (any one of: low-power hardware or radios, sleep most of the time, energy harvesting).
Why energy matters: batteries are hard to service at this scale (any one of: replacing or recharging 100,000 batteries is slow, costly, impractical).

questions.explanation: Model answer: For security, every sensor should get a unique password and regular security updates. For interoperability, the city should require open standards or use gateways that translate between protocols. For energy, the sensors should use low-power radios and sleep most of the time, waking up only to send data. Energy matters so much because replacing 100,000 batteries would be slow and expensive.

questions.content: Which IoT component connects local devices to the internet and can translate between protocols?
questions.explanation: A gateway connects local devices to the internet and can translate, for example, from Zigbee to Wi-Fi.

questions.content: What is an IoT node usually built around?
questions.explanation: An IoT node is usually built around a microcontroller with a radio.

questions.content: In an IoT system, what is the main job of the cloud or server platform?
options: To store and analyse data from the devices
To measure the room temperature directly
To physically switch the lights on and off
To supply power to battery-powered devices
questions.explanation: The cloud or server platform stores and analyses the data; sensors measure and actuators act.

questions.content: What are the three layers of the basic IoT architecture?
questions.explanation: The basic three-layer IoT architecture has a perception layer, a network layer and an application layer.

questions.content: Which layer of the three-layer IoT architecture contains the sensors and actuators?
questions.explanation: The perception (sensing) layer contains the sensors and actuators.

questions.content: Which layer does the five-layer IoT architecture add between the network and application layers?
questions.explanation: The five-layer architecture adds a processing layer (middleware) between the network and application layers.

questions.content: In which IoT communication model do devices talk directly to each other, for example a switch and a bulb over Bluetooth?
questions.explanation: In the device-to-device model, devices communicate directly with each other.

questions.content: In a home automation system, a motion sensor detects a person and the hall light turns on. What is the role of the light?
options: An actuator that acts on a command
A gateway that links two networks
A broker that routes the messages
questions.explanation: The light changes the physical world when it receives a command, so it is an actuator.

questions.content: Smart bulbs in a house use Zigbee, but the cloud service can only be reached over Wi-Fi. Which component solves this?
options: A second Zigbee bulb next to the Wi-Fi router
A larger battery inside every one of the bulbs
A hub that translates between Zigbee and Wi-Fi
A mobile app that shows the status of the bulbs
questions.explanation: A gateway (hub) connects local devices to the internet and translates between protocols.

questions.content: A team is choosing between Wi-Fi, LoRa and cellular to send sensor data to a server. Which layer of the three-layer architecture are they designing?
questions.explanation: The network layer transmits data using technologies such as Wi-Fi, cellular networks, Zigbee or LoRa.

questions.content: A system must store and analyse terabytes of sensor data before showing results in an app. In the five-layer architecture, which layer does this work?
questions.explanation: The processing layer (middleware) stores, analyses and processes large amounts of data.

questions.content: A smart parking app shows drivers where the free parking spaces are. Which layer of the IoT architecture does the app belong to?
questions.explanation: The application layer delivers services, such as a smart parking app, to users.

questions.content: A fitness band sends data via Bluetooth to the owner's phone, and the phone uploads it to the cloud. Which communication model is this?
questions.explanation: The phone acts as a local gateway that forwards the band's data to the cloud.

questions.content: A thermostat company shares its users' energy data, with their permission, with the electricity provider's platform. Which communication model is this?
questions.explanation: Data collected in one cloud service is shared with another authorised service: back-end data sharing.

questions.content: Explain what sensors, actuators and a gateway each do in an IoT system.

rubric.text: Sensors measure physical quantities
Actuators change the physical world
A gateway links local devices to the internet (any one of: connects them to the internet, translates protocols, forwards their data).

questions.explanation: Model answer: Sensors measure the physical world, for example temperature. Actuators change it, for example by switching a relay. A gateway connects the local devices to the internet and translates between protocols such as Zigbee and Wi-Fi.

questions.content: In the three-layer IoT architecture, which layer is at the bottom and which is at the top? Describe what the bottom layer does.

rubric.text: The lowest layer is the perception layer
The top layer is the application layer
The bottom layer collects data from the physical world (any one of: with sensors, with actuators, senses the environment).

questions.explanation: Model answer: The lowest layer is the perception layer. It uses sensors and actuators to collect data from the physical world. The top layer is the application layer, which delivers services to users.

questions.content: Explain the difference between the device-to-cloud and the device-to-gateway communication models.

rubric.text: Device-to-cloud: the device connects directly to a cloud service
Device-to-gateway (both needed: a local gateway such as a hub or phone; it forwards the data onward to the cloud).

questions.explanation: Model answer: In the device-to-cloud model, the device connects directly to a cloud service over the internet, for example through Wi-Fi. In the device-to-gateway model, the device connects to a local hub or smartphone, which forwards the data to the cloud.

questions.content: Explain why low power consumption and scalability are important design goals for IoT systems.

rubric.text: Low power: many devices run on batteries for a long time
Scalability: a system may grow very large (any one of: millions of devices, large volumes of data).

questions.explanation: Model answer: Low power consumption matters because many devices run on batteries that must last for years. Scalability matters because a system may grow to millions of devices that produce large volumes of data.

questions.content: Design a home automation system that turns on the hall light when someone enters at night. Describe the components and map them to the three architecture layers.

rubric.text: A motion sensor detects the person
A smart bulb or relay is the actuator
The network layer carries the data (any one of: via the hub, via the gateway, over Zigbee or Wi-Fi).
Perception layer mapping (both needed: the motion sensor; the smart bulb or relay).
The rule runs in the application layer

questions.explanation: Model answer: A motion sensor detects a person, and a smart bulb is the actuator that switches the light. The sensor and the bulb belong to the perception layer. They talk to a hub over Zigbee, and the network layer carries the data to the cloud. The rule that turns on the light at night runs in the application layer.

questions.content: Describe the five-layer IoT architecture layer by layer, and explain what the two extra layers add compared with the three-layer model.

rubric.text: Perception layer: sensors collect data
Network layer: transmits the data
Processing layer: handles large amounts of data (any one of: stores, analyses, processes).
Application layer: delivers services to users
Business layer: manages the whole system (any one of: overall management, business models, privacy).

questions.explanation: Model answer: The perception layer has sensors and actuators that collect data. The network layer transmits the data. The processing layer, or middleware, stores and analyses large amounts of data. The application layer delivers services to users. The business layer manages the whole system, including business models and privacy.

questions.content: Which messaging model does MQTT use?
questions.explanation: MQTT uses a publish/subscribe model with a central broker.

questions.content: In MQTT, what is the server that receives messages and forwards them to subscribers called?
questions.explanation: Clients send messages to a central server called a broker, which forwards them to subscribers.

questions.content: What is the default port for MQTT without TLS?
questions.explanation: MQTT uses port 1883 by default and 8883 over TLS; 5683 is the CoAP port.

questions.content: Which MQTT QoS level delivers a message exactly once?
questions.explanation: QoS 2 uses a four-step handshake to deliver a message exactly once; there is no QoS 3.

questions.content: What does the broker do with a retained message?
options: Stores it and sends it to new subscribers of the topic
Deletes it after the first subscriber reads it
Sends it back only to the client that published it
Hides it until the publisher connects again
questions.explanation: A retained message is stored for its topic and sent immediately to new subscribers.

questions.content: Which transport protocol does CoAP use by default?
questions.explanation: Unlike HTTP, CoAP runs over UDP, by default on port 5683.

questions.content: Which CoAP message type must be acknowledged by the receiver?
questions.explanation: Confirmable messages must be acknowledged with an ACK and are retransmitted if no ACK arrives.

questions.content: A client subscribes to the topic home/+/temperature. Which published topic will it receive?
questions.explanation: The plus sign matches exactly one level, so only home/<one level>/temperature matches.

questions.content: Which subscription receives every message published under home, at any depth?
questions.explanation: The hash sign matches all remaining levels and must be the last character.

questions.content: A sensor sends a temperature reading every second, and losing one reading does not matter. Which QoS level is the most efficient choice?
questions.explanation: QoS 0 (at most once) has no acknowledgement overhead; an occasional lost reading is acceptable here.

questions.content: A door lock must receive the 'unlock' command once and only once, even on an unreliable network. Which QoS level fits?
questions.explanation: Only QoS 2 guarantees exactly-once delivery; QoS 1 may deliver the command twice.

questions.content: A monitoring app wants to know when a sensor goes offline unexpectedly. Which MQTT feature should the sensor set when it connects?
questions.explanation: The broker publishes the Last Will message if the client disconnects unexpectedly.

questions.content: A client sends a CoAP GET request for /temperature and the resource exists. Which response code is typical?
questions.explanation: 2.05 Content returns the resource; 4.04 means it does not exist.

questions.content: A dashboard must be told every time a sensor's value changes, without sending repeated GET requests. Which CoAP feature helps?
questions.explanation: With the Observe option, the server sends notifications whenever the resource changes.

questions.content: Explain how messages travel from one client to another in MQTT.

rubric.text: Messages go through a central broker
A client publishes a message to a topic
The broker forwards the message to the subscribers

questions.explanation: Model answer: In MQTT, clients do not send messages directly to each other. A client publishes a message to a topic on a central broker, and the broker forwards it to every client that has subscribed to that topic.

questions.content: Compare MQTT QoS 0 and QoS 1.

rubric.text: QoS 0 (both needed: delivered at most once or without acknowledgement; the message may be lost).
QoS 1 (both needed: delivered at least once or acknowledged with PUBACK; the message may be duplicated).

questions.explanation: Model answer: QoS 0 means at most once: the message is sent without acknowledgement, so it may be lost. QoS 1 means at least once: the sender keeps the message until it gets a PUBACK, so it arrives but may be duplicated.

questions.content: Why does CoAP define both Confirmable and Non-confirmable messages?

rubric.text: CoAP runs over unreliable UDP
Confirmable messages (both needed: acknowledged with an ACK; retransmitted if no ACK arrives).
Non-confirmable messages are not acknowledged, which saves resources (any one of: energy, bandwidth, fewer messages).

questions.explanation: Model answer: CoAP runs over UDP, which is unreliable. Confirmable messages must be acknowledged with an ACK and are retransmitted if no ACK arrives. Non-confirmable messages are not acknowledged, which saves energy and bandwidth for data that can be lost.

questions.content: Give two ways in which CoAP is similar to HTTP and one way in which it is different.

rubric.text: Both follow the REST style: resources identified by URIs
Like HTTP, CoAP uses requests with methods or codes (any one of: methods such as GET or POST, similar response codes).
CoAP differs in transport or size (any one of: runs over UDP instead of TCP, small 4-byte header).

questions.explanation: Model answer: Like HTTP, CoAP follows the REST style and identifies resources with URIs. It also uses methods such as GET and POST and response codes similar to HTTP. Unlike HTTP, CoAP runs over UDP instead of TCP.

questions.content: Design the MQTT messaging for a smart greenhouse with a temperature sensor and a fan in each of three rooms. Give example topics, a subscription that lets one dashboard read all rooms, and the delivery guarantee you would use for sensor data and for fan commands.

rubric.text: All messages go through one broker
Each room has its own topic level (any one of: greenhouse/<room>/temperature, one topic per room).
The dashboard subscribes with the single-level wildcard (any one of: +, plus sign, matches one level).
Sensor data: QoS 0 (at most once)
Fan commands: QoS 1 or QoS 2

questions.explanation: Model answer: All devices connect to one broker. Each room publishes to its own topic, for example greenhouse/room1/temperature, and each fan subscribes to a command topic such as greenhouse/room1/fan. The dashboard subscribes to greenhouse/+/temperature, where the plus sign matches one level, so it gets all rooms. Sensor readings use QoS 0, because a lost reading is replaced a second later. Fan commands use QoS 1, so a command is not lost.

questions.content: A battery-powered sensor network must choose between MQTT and CoAP. Compare the two protocols and recommend one for a device that only answers occasional requests from a server.

rubric.text: MQTT runs over TCP
MQTT needs a broker
CoAP is light on the network (any one of: runs over UDP, small 4-byte header).
CoAP follows the REST style
Recommends CoAP

questions.explanation: Model answer: MQTT runs over TCP and needs a broker, and devices keep a connection open. CoAP runs over UDP with a small 4-byte header, which saves energy. CoAP follows the REST style, where a server reads a resource with GET. For a device that only answers occasional requests, I recommend CoAP, because it needs no broker and no open TCP connection.

questions.content: Which of these sensors needs an external excitation (power) source to produce its output?
questions.explanation: An RTD's resistance can only be read by passing a current through it; the other three generate their own signal.

questions.content: Which of these is an example of a self-generating sensor?
questions.explanation: A thermocouple produces its own small voltage from heat; resistive sensors need an excitation current.

questions.content: In a capacitive MEMS accelerometer, what changes when the device accelerates?
options: The capacitance between the moving mass and the fixed plates
The resistance of a platinum wire wrapped around the frame
The voltage produced at the junction of two different metals
The time of flight of an ultrasonic echo inside the chip
questions.explanation: The proof mass moves relative to the fixed plates, which changes the capacitance between them.

questions.content: How does an ultrasonic proximity sensor work out the distance to an object?
options: From the change in inductance caused by a nearby metal object
From the time of flight of an echo: speed of sound x time / 2
From the change in resistance of a heated thin metal film
From the voltage generated at a junction of two metals
questions.explanation: An ultrasonic sensor times the echo; the sound travels there and back, so the distance is speed x time / 2.

questions.content: What does the sensitivity of a sensor describe?
options: The smallest input that gives any output from zero
The span between the lowest and highest measurable value
The change in output per unit change in input
How long the output takes to settle after a change
questions.explanation: Sensitivity is the slope of the response, for example 10 mV per degC.

questions.content: Which characteristic describes how close a reading is to the true value?
questions.explanation: Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated readings to each other.

questions.content: What is the threshold of a sensor?
options: The smallest input, starting from zero, that gives a detectable output
The largest input the sensor can measure before it saturates
The time the sensor needs to reach 63% of its final output
The largest deviation of the output from a straight line
questions.explanation: Threshold is the minimum input from zero that produces a detectable output.

questions.content: A temperature sensor is read by passing a small current through it and measuring the voltage. Which group does it belong to?
options: Self-generating, because it produces its own voltage from the heat
Externally excited, because it needs an excitation to give an output
Digital, because the measured voltage is later sent to an ADC
Non-contact, because it does not need to touch the object
questions.explanation: A sensor that needs an excitation current to be read is an externally excited sensor.

questions.content: Why is a thermocouple a better choice than an NTC thermistor for monitoring a furnace at about 1000 degC?
options: A thermocouple gives a much larger output voltage than a thermistor
A thermocouple's resistance falls sharply as the temperature rises
A thermocouple works over a very wide range, up to more than 1000 degC
A thermocouple needs no amplifier because its signal is already large
questions.explanation: Thermocouples cover very wide ranges; thermistors are sensitive but work over a limited range.

questions.content: An inductive proximity sensor fails to detect an object on a production line. Which object is most likely?
questions.explanation: Inductive sensors detect metal objects through a change in inductance; plastic does not affect it.

questions.content: Repeated readings of the same 25.0 degC bath give 26.1, 26.0 and 26.1 degC. How would you describe this sensor?
questions.explanation: The readings agree closely with each other (precise) but are about 1 degC from the true value (not accurate).

questions.content: A humidity sensor reads 62% when humidity rises to 60%, but 58% when humidity falls to 60%. Which characteristic does this show?
questions.explanation: The reading for the same input depends on the direction of change, which is hysteresis.

questions.content: A gas sensor meant for carbon monoxide also changes its output when the humidity changes. Which characteristic is poor?
questions.explanation: Specificity (selectivity) means responding only to the intended quantity.

questions.content: A sensor is placed in hot water and takes 20 s to reach 90% of its final reading. What does this figure describe?
questions.explanation: Response time is how long the output takes to reach (a set fraction of) its final value after a step change.

questions.content: Sensors can be grouped by whether they need an external power source. Explain the difference between the two groups and give one example of each.

rubric.text: One group needs an excitation to give an output (any one of: external excitation, a power supply, a current must be passed through it). The label active or passive is not required.
The other group generates its own signal (any one of: self-generating, produces its own voltage, no external power needed). The label active or passive is not required.
Examples (both needed: an excited sensor such as a thermistor, RTD or strain gauge; a self-generating sensor such as a thermocouple, solar cell or piezoelectric sensor).

questions.explanation: Model answer: One group needs an external excitation to give an output; for example, a thermistor can only be read by passing a current through it. The other group is self-generating: it generates its own signal from the energy it measures; for example, a thermocouple produces its own small voltage from heat.

questions.content: Explain the difference between the accuracy and the precision of a sensor.

rubric.text: Accuracy is closeness to the true value (any one of: close to the true value, close to the actual value, small error from the real value).
Precision is closeness of repeated readings to each other (any one of: repeatability, consistent readings, small spread).

questions.explanation: Model answer: Accuracy is how close a reading is to the true value of the quantity. Precision is how close repeated readings of the same input are to each other, so a sensor can be precise but not accurate.

questions.content: What is hysteresis in a sensor, and why can it be a problem for the readings?

rubric.text: The output for the same input depends on the direction of change (any one of: increasing versus decreasing input, rising versus falling, depends on the previous value).
Problem: the same input can give different readings (any one of: two possible readings, an error of up to the hysteresis width, the reading is not unique).

questions.explanation: Model answer: Hysteresis means that the output for the same input depends on whether the input was increasing or decreasing. It is a problem because the same true value can give different readings, which adds an error.

questions.content: Explain how a capacitive MEMS accelerometer turns acceleration into an electrical signal.

rubric.text: A proof mass on springs moves when the device accelerates (any one of: the mass moves, the mass shifts, the springs bend).
The movement changes the capacitance of the plates (any one of: capacitance changes, one capacitance rises while the other falls).
The readout measures this change to obtain the acceleration (any one of: the change is proportional to the acceleration, the circuit converts it to a voltage).

questions.explanation: Model answer: A capacitive MEMS accelerometer has a tiny proof mass held by springs. When the device accelerates, the mass moves relative to the frame, and this changes the capacitance between the mass and the fixed plates. The readout circuit measures the change, which is proportional to the acceleration.

questions.content: A cold-storage room must be kept between -30 degC and +10 degC with small temperature changes detected, and a furnace must be monitored up to 1000 degC where temperature can jump quickly. Which type of temperature sensor would you choose for each place? Justify each choice by range or response time.

rubric.text: Cold room: a thermistor or RTD (any one of: thermistor, RTD, platinum RTD, IC temperature sensor).
Reason for the cold room (any one of: narrow range is enough, high sensitivity, accurate, stable).
Furnace: a thermocouple.
Reason for the furnace by range (any one of: very wide range, works above 1000 degC, survives high temperature).
Reason by response time (any one of: a small junction responds quickly, fast response, follows sudden jumps).

questions.explanation: Model answer: For the cold room I would choose a thermistor, because the range is narrow and a thermistor is very sensitive, so small changes are detected. For the furnace I would choose a thermocouple, because it works over a very wide range up to more than 1000 degC, and a thermocouple with a small junction responds quickly to sudden jumps.

questions.content: A greenhouse controller switches a fan on at 70 %RH. Two humidity sensors are offered. Sensor Alpha: accuracy +/-2 %RH, hysteresis 1 %RH, non-linearity 0.5 %RH. Sensor Beta: accuracy +/-5 %RH, hysteresis 4 %RH, non-linearity 3 %RH. Which sensor would you choose, and what would each of Beta's three figures mean for when the fan switches?

rubric.text: Chooses Alpha.
Beta's accuracy: the fan may switch anywhere from about 65 to 75 %RH (any one of: up to 5 %RH from the true humidity, switches too early or too late).
Beta's hysteresis: the switching point depends on whether humidity is rising or falling (any one of: different point when rising than falling, up to 4 %RH apart).
Beta's non-linearity: the error is different at different humidity levels (any one of: error changes across the range, readings do not follow a straight line).

questions.explanation: Model answer: I would choose Alpha. With Beta, the accuracy of +/-5 %RH means the fan could switch anywhere from about 65 to 75 %RH. Its hysteresis of 4 %RH means the switching point is different when humidity is rising than when it is falling. Its non-linearity means the error changes across the range, so the readings do not follow a straight line.

questions.content: In a typical sensor readout chain, which block scales the sensor voltage to the ADC's input range?
options: An amplifier built with an operational amplifier
The microcontroller that processes the digital codes
The communication module that sends data to the cloud
The reference voltage source inside the ADC chip
questions.explanation: An opamp amplifier scales the small sensor voltage to the ADC's input range.

questions.content: What are the two steps an ADC performs?
questions.explanation: An ADC samples the signal at regular instants and quantizes each sample to a digital code.

questions.content: How many output codes does a 10-bit ADC have?
questions.explanation: An N-bit ADC has 2^N codes; 2^10 = 1024.

questions.content: What is the size of one LSB for an N-bit ADC with reference voltage Vref?
questions.explanation: The full-scale range Vref is divided into 2^N steps, so one LSB = Vref / 2^N.

questions.content: What is the minimum sampling rate needed to capture a signal whose highest frequency is f?
questions.explanation: The Nyquist criterion requires a sampling rate of more than twice the highest signal frequency.

questions.content: With rounding to the nearest level, what is the largest quantization error of an ADC?
questions.explanation: Rounding to the nearest level gives an error of at most half an LSB.

questions.content: What happens when the input voltage of an ADC goes above its full-scale range?
options: The ADC adds extra bits automatically
The output wraps around to zero and counts again
The output saturates at the maximum code
The sampling rate doubles to follow the signal
questions.explanation: Above full scale the ADC clips: every such input gives the maximum code.

questions.content: A 50 mV sensor signal is fed directly into an ADC with a 5 V range. What is the main problem?
options: The ADC is damaged because the input voltage is far above its full-scale range
The sampling rate becomes too low because the signal voltage is very small
The ADC output saturates at the maximum code for every input value
Only about 1% of the range is used, so few codes change and resolution is poor
questions.explanation: A small signal uses only a tiny part of the ADC range; amplifying it first improves the effective resolution.

questions.content: An 8-bit ADC has Vref = 2.048 V. What is its LSB?
A vibration signal contains frequencies up to 500 Hz. Which sampling rate is the lowest that still avoids aliasing?
questions.explanation: The rate must be more than 2 x 500 Hz = 1000 samples per second; of these choices only 1200 is high enough.

questions.content: A sensor has a sensitivity of 20 mV per degC and the ADC's LSB is 2 mV. What temperature change does one LSB represent?
questions.explanation: Resolution in the measured quantity = LSB / sensitivity = 2 mV / 20 mV per degC = 0.1 degC.

questions.content: Moving from a 10-bit to a 12-bit ADC with the same Vref has which effect?
options: The LSB becomes two times larger
The full-scale range becomes four times larger
The sampling rate becomes four times higher
The LSB becomes four times smaller
questions.explanation: Two more bits give 2^2 = 4 times as many codes over the same range, so the LSB is four times smaller.

questions.content: Which is a typical cost of choosing an ADC with many more bits than the application needs?
options: More power, slower conversion and more data
A larger quantization error at every sample
A smaller full-scale input range for the sensor
A lower sensitivity of the sensor itself
questions.explanation: More bits give finer resolution but usually cost more power, conversion time, price and data.

questions.content: Why is the amplifier gain chosen so that the largest sensor signal stays just below the ADC full scale?
options: To make the sampling rate as low as possible
To use most of the ADC range without saturating
To remove the need for a reference voltage
To make the quantization error larger than one LSB
questions.explanation: A gain close to full scale uses most ADC codes (best resolution) while avoiding clipping.

questions.content: Why does a sensor readout chain usually amplify the sensor signal before the ADC?

rubric.text: Sensor signals are often small (any one of: millivolts, microvolts, a weak signal).
Without amplification only a small part of the ADC range is used (any one of: few codes change, poor resolution, most of the range is unused).
Amplifying scales the signal to the ADC's full range (any one of: use the full scale, match the ADC input range).

questions.explanation: Model answer: Sensor signals are often small, only millivolts or microvolts. Fed directly into an ADC, such a signal uses only a small part of the range, so few codes change and the resolution is poor. Amplifying first scales the signal to the ADC's full range.

questions.content: What is quantization in an ADC, and how large can the quantization error be?

rubric.text: Quantization maps each sample to one of a limited number of levels (any one of: nearest level, rounding, discrete steps).
The error is at most half an LSB (any one of: half an LSB, LSB / 2, 0.5 LSB).

questions.explanation: Model answer: Quantization maps each sampled value to the nearest of the ADC's discrete levels, so the input becomes a staircase. With rounding to the nearest level, the quantization error is at most half an LSB.

questions.content: How fast must an ADC sample a signal, and what goes wrong if it samples too slowly?

rubric.text: Sample faster than twice the highest signal frequency (any one of: more than twice, more than 2f, double the highest frequency).
Too slow causes aliasing (any one of: the signal appears at a wrong lower frequency, fast changes are missed, the signal is distorted).

questions.explanation: Model answer: The ADC must sample at more than twice the highest frequency in the signal. If it samples too slowly, fast changes are missed and the signal appears at a wrong, lower frequency, which is called aliasing.

questions.content: What do you gain and what do you lose when you choose an ADC with more bits?

rubric.text: Gain: a smaller LSB (any one of: finer resolution, more levels, smaller steps).
Loss (any one of: more power, slower conversion, higher cost, more data).

questions.explanation: Model answer: More bits give a smaller LSB, so the resolution is finer. The cost is that the ADC usually uses more power, converts more slowly, is more expensive and produces more data.

questions.content: A temperature sensor outputs 10 mV per degC. It is read by a 12-bit ADC with a full-scale reference of 4.096 V. Calculate the LSB size and the smallest temperature change the system can resolve, showing your method.

rubric.text: Method for the LSB (any one of: Vref / 2^N, 4.096 / 4096, divide 4.096 V by 2^12).
Result: LSB = 1 mV.
Method for the temperature resolution (any one of: LSB / sensitivity, 1 mV / 10 mV per degC).
Result: 0.1 degC.

questions.explanation: Model answer: The LSB is Vref / 2^N = 4.096 V / 4096 = 1 mV. The temperature resolution is the LSB divided by the sensitivity: 1 mV / 10 mV per degC = 0.1 degC.

questions.content: A pressure sensor gives 0 to 100 mV. The ADC input range is 0 to 4.096 V. Choose an amplifier gain that uses the ADC range well without saturating it, and explain your choice.

rubric.text: Method (any one of: gain = ADC range / largest sensor signal, 4.096 / 0.1, 4096 mV / 100 mV).
Result: a gain of about 40, no more than 40.96.
Reason: it uses most of the ADC range (any one of: best resolution, most codes used, close to full scale).
A higher gain would saturate the ADC (any one of: clipping, exceeds 4.096 V, output stuck at the maximum code).

questions.explanation: Model answer: The gain is the ADC range divided by the largest sensor signal: 4.096 V / 0.1 V = 40.96, so I choose a gain of 40. This uses most of the ADC range, which gives the best resolution. A higher gain such as 41 would give 4.1 V, which exceeds 4.096 V and would saturate the ADC.

questions.content: Which of these is a property of an ideal opamp?
questions.explanation: An ideal opamp has infinite input resistance, infinite open-loop gain, infinite bandwidth and zero offset.

questions.content: In readout design, what is a non-ideality?
options: A sensor that measures more than one physical quantity at the same time
A digital code that the ADC cannot produce because of saturation
A sampling rate that is lower than twice the signal frequency
A way a real opamp differs from an ideal one, adding an error to the reading
questions.explanation: Non-idealities are the differences between a real and an ideal opamp; each adds an error.

questions.content: What is the loading effect in a sensor readout?
options: The amplifier's input resistance draws current, so part of the sensor voltage is lost
The ADC rounds every sample to the nearest discrete level of its range
The sensor output changes when the measured quantity changes direction
The opamp output cannot go beyond the voltages of its power supply
questions.explanation: Rs and Rin form a voltage divider, so the amplifier sees only Vs x Rin / (Rs + Rin).

questions.content: Which circuit is commonly placed between a high-resistance sensor and the rest of the readout to avoid loading?
questions.explanation: A buffer has gain 1 and very high input resistance, so it draws almost no current from the sensor.

questions.content: What is the input offset voltage of an opamp?
options: The largest voltage the output can reach before it saturates
The maximum rate at which the output voltage can change
A small DC voltage that acts as if it were added to the input
The voltage lost across the sensor's output resistance
questions.explanation: Offset makes the output non-zero when the input is zero.

questions.content: What is the slew rate of an opamp?
options: The gain it has with no feedback applied
The small current flowing into its input pins
The range of voltages its output can reach
The maximum rate at which its output voltage can change
questions.explanation: Slew rate limits how fast the output can change; faster, large signals are distorted.

questions.content: What does the gain-bandwidth product of an opamp imply?
options: Higher gain means a lower frequency at which the gain starts to fall
Higher gain means the output can swing beyond the supply voltages
Higher gain means the input offset voltage becomes smaller
Higher gain means the input resistance becomes much higher
questions.explanation: Gain x bandwidth is roughly constant, so raising the gain lowers the usable bandwidth.

questions.content: A sensor with Rs = 1 kOhm is connected to an amplifier with Rin = 1 MOhm. About how much of the sensor voltage does the amplifier see?
questions.explanation: Rin / (Rs + Rin) = 1000 / 1001, about 99.9%; Rin is much larger than Rs, so loading is negligible.

questions.content: A sensor reading is clearly too low when the sensor is connected to the amplifier, but correct when measured with a very high-resistance meter. What is the most likely cause?
options: The ADC's number of bits is too high for the size of the sensor signal
The sampling rate is more than twice the highest frequency of the signal
The amplifier's input resistance is not much larger than the sensor's output resistance
The opamp's slew rate is too high for the slowly changing sensor signal
questions.explanation: The amplifier loads the sensor; a buffer or a higher-input-resistance opamp fixes it.

questions.content: An amplifier with a gain of 100 uses an opamp with a 1 mV input offset. What error does the offset cause at the output?
questions.explanation: The offset is multiplied by the gain: 1 mV x 100 = 0.1 V.

questions.content: For which sensor does the opamp's input bias current matter most?
options: One with a very high output resistance
One with a very low output resistance
One that already has a digital output
One that is read only once a day
questions.explanation: Bias current flowing through a large source resistance creates a large error voltage.

questions.content: An amplifier designed with resistors for a gain of 1000 measures a gain of 990. Which non-ideality explains this best?
questions.explanation: Because the open-loop gain is not infinite, the closed-loop gain is slightly lower than designed.

questions.content: A large, fast audio-frequency signal comes out of an amplifier with sloped, triangular edges instead of its true shape. Which limit is most likely reached?
questions.explanation: When the output cannot change fast enough, large fast signals are distorted by the slew rate.

questions.content: An amplifier's output stays stuck at the supply voltage whenever the sensor signal is large. What is happening?
options: The input bias current is flowing through the feedback resistors
The open-loop gain has become infinite at large input signals
The input offset voltage cancels out the sensor signal completely
The output is saturating because it cannot swing beyond the supply
questions.explanation: The output cannot go beyond the supply voltages, so a too-large signal saturates.

questions.content: What is the input offset voltage of an opamp, and why does it matter more when the amplifier gain is large?

rubric.text: Offset is a small DC voltage that acts as if added to the input (any one of: output not zero for a zero input, a small error voltage at the input).
The gain multiplies the offset (any one of: amplified by the gain, a large output error).

questions.explanation: Model answer: The input offset voltage is a small DC voltage that acts as if it were added to the input, so the output is not zero when the input is zero. The amplifier multiplies the offset by its gain, so with a large gain it becomes a large output error.

questions.content: What is the input bias current of an opamp, and why is it a problem for sensors with a high output resistance?

rubric.text: A small current flows into the opamp's input pins (any one of: current into the inputs, the opamp draws a small current).
It flows through the source resistance, creating an error voltage (any one of: voltage drop across the sensor resistance, larger error for high resistance).

questions.explanation: Model answer: The input bias current is a small current that flows into the opamp's input pins. It flows through the sensor's source resistance and creates an error voltage, which is large when the resistance is high.

questions.content: Why is the real gain of an opamp amplifier slightly different from the gain set by its resistors?

rubric.text: The open-loop gain of a real opamp is not infinite (any one of: finite open-loop gain, limited open-loop gain).
So the closed-loop gain is slightly lower than designed (any one of: lower, smaller, a small gain error).

questions.explanation: Model answer: A real opamp's open-loop gain is finite, not infinite. Because of this, the closed-loop gain of the amplifier is slightly lower than the value set by its resistors.

questions.content: Why can an opamp fail to amplify a fast-changing sensor signal correctly? Name the two limits involved and what each does.

rubric.text: Limited bandwidth: the gain falls at high frequencies (any one of: gain-bandwidth product, higher gain means lower bandwidth, high frequencies are attenuated).
Slew rate: the output can change only at a maximum rate (any one of: cannot change fast enough, large fast signals are distorted).

questions.explanation: Model answer: The first limit is the bandwidth: because the gain-bandwidth product is constant, the gain falls at high frequencies. The second is the slew rate: the output can change only at a maximum rate, so large, fast signals are distorted.

questions.content: A sensor behaves like a voltage source with an output resistance of 10 kOhm. It is connected to an amplifier with an input resistance of 90 kOhm. What fraction of the sensor voltage does the amplifier see? Explain why, and suggest how to fix the problem.

rubric.text: Method: the two resistances form a voltage divider (any one of: Rin / (Rs + Rin), 90 / (10 + 90), 90 kOhm / 100 kOhm).
Result: 90%.
Why: current flows through the sensor's output resistance (any one of: voltage drop across Rs, loading effect, Rin is not much larger than Rs).
Fix (any one of: a buffer or voltage follower, a much higher input resistance, an opamp with CMOS or FET inputs).

questions.explanation: Model answer: The output resistance and the input resistance form a voltage divider, so the amplifier sees Rin / (Rs + Rin) = 90 / (10 + 90) = 90% of the sensor voltage. Current flows through the sensor's output resistance and 10% of the voltage is lost across it, because Rin is not much larger than Rs. To fix it, put a buffer (voltage follower) with a very high input resistance between the sensor and the amplifier.

questions.content: A gas sensor has a very high output resistance of about 10 MOhm, its signal changes slowly over minutes, and it is read by an opamp amplifier. Which opamp property matters MOST here, and which matters LEAST? Explain both.

rubric.text: Most important (any one of: very high input resistance, very low input bias current, CMOS or FET inputs).
Reason: with a 10 MOhm source, current into the opamp causes a large error (any one of: loading loses voltage, bias current makes a large voltage drop).
Least important: bandwidth or slew rate.
Reason: the signal changes slowly (any one of: slow signal, low frequency, changes over minutes).

questions.explanation: Model answer: The input resistance, or equivalently a very low input bias current, matters most. With a 10 MOhm source, any current the opamp draws makes a large voltage drop across the sensor resistance and a large error. The bandwidth and slew rate matter least, because the signal changes slowly over minutes, so it is a very low frequency signal.

questions.content: Predicting that a machine will fail before it actually happens, using its sensor data, is called what?
questions.explanation: Predicting failures before they happen from sensor data is predictive maintenance.

questions.content: Which goal of IoT data analysis means finding readings that do not fit the normal pattern?
questions.explanation: Anomaly detection finds readings that do not fit the normal pattern, such as a sudden spike.

questions.content: In the components of learning, what is the hypothesis set?
options: The unknown function that truly maps inputs to outputs
The table of past input and output examples collected
The family of candidate models the algorithm may choose from
The error the final model makes on new, unseen data
questions.explanation: The hypothesis set is the family of candidate models, for example all straight lines.

questions.content: What is the error of a model on new, unseen data called?
questions.explanation: In-sample error is on the training data; out-of-sample error is on new, unseen data.

questions.content: Which type of learning uses training examples that each come with the correct answer?
questions.explanation: Supervised learning uses labelled examples; unsupervised learning has no labels.

questions.content: Which type of learning lets an agent learn by trial and error from rewards?
questions.explanation: Reinforcement learning learns from rewards, such as a thermostat learning from comfort feedback.

questions.content: Which Python library is mainly used to handle tables of data, such as sensor logs?
questions.explanation: pandas handles tables; NumPy handles arrays, scikit-learn provides models and matplotlib draws plots.

questions.content: Why does IoT data analysis often use machine learning instead of hand-written rules?
options: Machine learning models need no data at all to make their predictions
Hand-written rules cannot run on any computer connected to the internet
Machine learning always gives perfect predictions on every sensor
The rules behind the data are often unknown or too complex to write by hand
questions.explanation: Machine learning learns a model from the data when the underlying rules are unknown or too complex.

questions.content: A model fits its training data almost perfectly but makes large errors on new data. What is this called?
questions.explanation: Fitting the training data including its noise but failing on new data is overfitting.

questions.content: According to the idea of feasibility of learning, when is a model that does well on its training data likely to do well on new data too?
options: When the model is as complex as possible so it fits every point
When the data are representative and there are enough examples
When the training data come from a single day of measurements
When the test data were also used to train the same model
questions.explanation: Learning is feasible when the data represent the situations of use and there are enough examples.

questions.content: Predicting tomorrow's energy use in kWh from past readings is which kind of task?
questions.explanation: The output is a number and past answers are known, so it is supervised regression.

questions.content: Labelling each motor as 'faulty' or 'normal' from its vibration features is which kind of task?
