questions.explanation: The output is a category learned from labelled examples, so it is classification.

questions.content: A temperature sensor occasionally reports 999 degC because of a loose wire. Which pipeline step should deal with this?
options: Data cleaning: remove or correct the outliers
Splitting the data into training and test sets
Choosing the number of clusters k
questions.explanation: Impossible values from faulty sensors are outliers, handled in the cleaning step.

questions.content: Computing the average vibration of a motor over each minute, to feed into a model, is which pipeline step?
questions.explanation: Turning raw readings into inputs such as a one-minute average is feature computation.

questions.content: Explain why raw IoT sensor readings need to be analysed, and what predictive maintenance and anomaly detection each achieve.

rubric.text: Raw readings are of little use until analysed (any one of: huge amounts of data, must be turned into information, needed for decisions).
Predictive maintenance predicts failures before they happen (any one of: repair in time, avoid breakdowns).
Anomaly detection finds readings that do not fit the normal pattern (any one of: unusual readings, a sudden spike, a sign of a fault or attack).

questions.explanation: Model answer: Raw sensor readings arrive in huge amounts and are of little use until they are analysed and turned into information and decisions. Predictive maintenance predicts machine failures before they happen, so repairs can be made in time. Anomaly detection finds readings that do not fit the normal pattern, such as a sudden spike that may mean a fault or an attack.

questions.content: Describe the components of learning from data: what is unknown, what we have, and what the learning algorithm produces.

rubric.text: An unknown target function maps inputs to outputs (any one of: target function, true function f, the real relationship we cannot see).
We have a data set of past examples (any one of: data set, examples of input with output, training data).
The algorithm picks a final hypothesis from a hypothesis set (any one of: chooses the best candidate model, the final model approximates the target function).

questions.explanation: Model answer: There is an unknown target function f that maps inputs to outputs. What we have is a data set of past examples of inputs with their outputs. The learning algorithm searches a hypothesis set of candidate models and picks the final hypothesis g that fits the data best, so that it approximates f.

questions.content: How do supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning differ in the kind of feedback the learner gets?

rubric.text: Supervised: every example has the correct answer (any one of: labels, labelled data, known outputs).
Unsupervised: no labels, finds structure by itself (any one of: no labels, groups similar data, finds patterns).
Reinforcement: learns from rewards (any one of: reward, learning by trial, feedback on actions).

questions.explanation: Model answer: In supervised learning every training example comes with the correct answer, a label. In unsupervised learning there are no labels, so the algorithm finds structure, such as groups, by itself. In reinforcement learning the agent learns by trial and error from rewards.

questions.content: Why is the data split into a training set and a test set before building a model?

rubric.text: The test set checks performance on data the model has not seen (any one of: unseen data, new data, how it will work in practice).
So the test set must be kept separate from training (any one of: kept aside, never used to fit the model, held out).

questions.explanation: Model answer: The training set is used to fit the model, and the test set checks how well the model works on data it has not seen, which is how it will be used in practice. For that, the test set must be kept aside and never used for training.

questions.content: A factory wants to predict motor failures from vibration sensors. Describe the data-driven pipeline from raw data to an action: how the data is prepared, which type of learning fits and why, and what the system does with a prediction.

rubric.text: Collect past data with labels (any one of: record which motors failed, labelled history).
Clean the data (any one of: handle missing values, remove outliers from faulty sensors).
Compute features (any one of: average vibration, RMS, peak value over a time window).
Type of learning (both needed: supervised classification or a classifier; because the past failures are labelled).
Action (any one of: raise an alert, schedule maintenance before failure, notify a technician).

questions.explanation: Model answer: First collect past vibration data and record which motors failed, so the data are labelled. Clean the data by handling missing values and removing outliers from faulty sensors. Compute features such as the average and peak vibration over each minute. Because the past failures are labelled, supervised classification fits. When the model predicts a failure, the system raises an alert and schedules maintenance before the motor breaks.

questions.content: A model that predicts a greenhouse's humidity was trained only on summer data. It works well in summer but makes large errors in winter. Using the idea of feasibility of learning, explain why, and suggest how to fix it.

rubric.text: The training data are not representative of winter (any one of: only summer conditions, the model never saw winter).
Low error on training data does not guarantee low error on new data (any one of: in-sample vs out-of-sample error, generalisation fails).
Fix: collect data from all seasons, then retrain (any one of: whole year of data, add winter data, retrain).
Check the model on winter test data before using it (any one of: test on winter, validate on new conditions).

questions.explanation: Model answer: Learning is only feasible when the training data are representative of the situations where the model is used; this model only saw summer conditions, so winter is not represented. Its low in-sample error does not guarantee a low out-of-sample error. To fix it, collect data from all seasons and retrain, then check the model on winter test data before using it.

questions.content: In the linear regression model y = w0 + w1 x, what does w1 represent?
options: The value of y when x is 0
The mean squared error of the fitted line
The slope: how much y changes when x increases by 1
The number of training examples used
questions.explanation: w1 is the slope; w0 is the intercept, the value of y when x is 0.

questions.content: How are the weights of a linear regression line chosen?
options: By maximising the number of clusters
By averaging the last few values of the series
By sorting the data by time before fitting
By minimising the mean squared error (least squares)
questions.explanation: Least squares chooses the weights that minimise the mean squared error.

questions.content: Which component of a time series is a pattern that repeats with a fixed period, such as a daily cycle?
questions.explanation: Seasonality repeats with a fixed period; the trend is a long-term increase or decrease.

questions.content: What does a moving average do to a time series?
options: It removes the time order of the readings
It smooths out noise so the trend is easier to see
It groups the readings into k clusters
It turns the readings into labels
questions.explanation: A moving average averages the last few values, which smooths noise.

questions.content: What does an autoregressive (AR) model use to predict the next value?
options: The distance to the nearest cluster centre
Only the value of a different, unrelated sensor
A weighted sum of previous values of the series
A random value drawn from the training data
questions.explanation: An AR model predicts the next value from previous values.

questions.content: Clustering is which type of learning?
questions.explanation: Clustering groups unlabelled data, so it is unsupervised.

questions.content: In k-means, what is each point assigned to in every iteration?
options: The cluster with the oldest data
questions.explanation: Each point is assigned to its nearest centroid, then the centroids move to the mean of their points.

questions.content: A line fitted as y = 1.5 + 0.2 x is used with x = 10. What is the prediction?
For the fitted line y = 1.5 + 0.2 x, what does the number 1.5 mean?
options: The change in y when x increases by 1
The mean squared error of the line
The predicted y when x is 0
The largest x used in training
questions.explanation: 1.5 is the intercept w0, the value of y when x is 0.

questions.content: Model A has a test MSE of 4.0 and model B has a test MSE of 9.0. Which predicts better?
options: It cannot be compared with MSE
questions.explanation: A smaller MSE means the predictions are closer to the actual values.

questions.content: A 24-hour moving average is drawn over three months of hourly temperatures. What does it mainly show?
options: The slow long-term movement, with the daily cycle smoothed out
Every individual daily peak more sharply than the raw data
Only the random noise left after removing the trend
The temperature forecast for the next three months
questions.explanation: Averaging a full day smooths the daily cycle and the noise, leaving the slow long-term movement.

questions.content: To capture a daily cycle in hourly temperature data, which extra input helps an AR model?
options: The value of a random other hour
questions.explanation: In hourly data the daily cycle repeats every 24 values, so the value 24 hours earlier helps.

questions.content: After clustering households by energy use, one new reading is far from every centroid. How can it be treated?
options: As the centre of a new largest cluster
As proof that k must be reduced to one
As a possible anomaly worth checking
As a reading that belongs to every cluster
questions.explanation: A point far from all centroids does not fit any normal group, so it can be flagged as an anomaly.

questions.content: In the elbow method, which k is usually chosen?
options: The largest k that was tried
The k that gives exactly one point per cluster
The k equal to the number of features
The k after which more clusters stop giving a large improvement
questions.explanation: The elbow is where adding clusters stops reducing the total distance much.

questions.content: What does linear regression find, and how is the line fitted to the data?

rubric.text: It finds a straight line relating the input to the output (any one of: a slope with an intercept, y = w0 + w1 x, a linear relationship).
The line is fitted by least squares (any one of: minimise the mean squared error, minimise squared differences, MSE).

questions.explanation: Model answer: Linear regression finds a straight line y = w0 + w1 x that describes how the output changes with the input. The line is fitted by least squares, choosing the weights that minimise the mean squared error between the predicted and actual values.

questions.content: Explain the three components that a time series is often described by.

rubric.text: Trend: a long-term rise or fall (any one of: long-term increase, long-term decrease, overall direction).
Seasonality: a pattern that repeats with a fixed period (any one of: daily cycle, weekly cycle, repeating pattern).
Noise: the random variation that is left (any one of: random, irregular, unpredictable).

questions.explanation: Model answer: The trend is the long-term increase or decrease. Seasonality is a pattern that repeats with a fixed period, such as a daily cycle. Noise is the random variation that is left over.

questions.content: Describe how the k-means algorithm groups data points once k starting centroids are chosen.

rubric.text: Assign every point to its nearest centroid (any one of: nearest, closest).
Move each centroid to the mean of its points (any one of: mean, average, update the centroid).
Repeat until the assignments stop changing (any one of: repeat, converge, stable).

questions.explanation: Model answer: Each point is assigned to its nearest centroid. Then each centroid is moved to the mean of the points assigned to it. These two steps are repeated until the assignments no longer change.

questions.content: Why should features usually be scaled before running k-means clustering?

rubric.text: k-means groups points by distance (any one of: distance, how far apart points are).
Unscaled, the feature with the larger range dominates (any one of: dominate, outweigh, gets more weight).

questions.explanation: Model answer: k-means groups points by their distance to the centroids. If the features are not scaled, the feature with the larger numeric range dominates the distances and the other features hardly matter.

questions.content: A building's daily energy use was modelled from outdoor temperatures between 10 and 35 degC as E = 2 + 0.5 T, with E in kWh and T in degC. Predict the energy use at 30 degC, showing your method; explain what the number 0.5 means; and say whether you would trust a prediction for 60 degC.

rubric.text: Method: substitute T = 30 into the line (any one of: 2 + 0.5 x 30, 0.5 times 30 plus 2).
Result: 17 kWh.
0.5 is the slope (any one of: energy rises 0.5 kWh per degree, per 1 degC increase).
60 degC is extrapolation, not to be trusted (any one of: outside the 10 to 35 range, beyond the data, the line may not stay linear).

questions.explanation: Model answer: Substituting T = 30 gives E = 2 + 0.5 x 30 = 17 kWh. The number 0.5 is the slope: the energy use rises by 0.5 kWh per degree. I would not trust a prediction for 60 degC, because it is outside the 10 to 35 degC range of the data; that is extrapolation, and the relationship may not stay linear.

questions.content: You must forecast the next hour's temperature in a greenhouse from hourly readings collected over three months, and the temperature has a clear daily cycle. How would you split the data for training and testing, which inputs would your model use, and why?

rubric.text: Split in time order: train on the earlier part, test on the later part.
Why (any one of: do not shuffle, the future must not leak into training, never test on the past using the future).
Inputs: previous hours' values (any one of: last few readings, autoregressive, lagged values).
Daily cycle: also the value from 24 hours earlier (any one of: 24-hour lag, same hour yesterday).

questions.explanation: Model answer: I would split the data in time order: train on the first two and a half months and test on the later part, and not shuffle, so the future never leaks into training. The model would be autoregressive, using the previous few hours' values, plus the value from 24 hours earlier to capture the daily cycle.

questions.content: Which key characteristic of IoT refers to systems with billions of connected devices?
questions.explanation: Very large scale means IoT systems can contain billions of devices.

questions.content: Which of these is an example of a thing sensing its environment?
options: A cloud server storing last month's readings
A sensor measuring the light level in a room
A phone app showing a chart of temperatures
A router forwarding packets to the internet
questions.explanation: Things sense their environment, for example temperature, motion or light.

questions.content: In a smart home, which task can a rule automate?
options: Choosing the vendor of each new device
Writing the firmware for the door lock
Turning off the lights when nobody is in a room
Replacing the batteries of every sensor
questions.explanation: Rules automate devices, such as turning off lights when nobody is in a room.

questions.content: Which smart-city service helps drivers find free spaces?
questions.explanation: Smart parking shows drivers where free spaces are.

questions.content: What can attackers build from many hijacked IoT devices?
questions.explanation: Attackers can take devices over and combine them into a botnet.

questions.content: A sensor sleeps for an hour to save energy and then rejoins the network. Which IoT characteristic does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Devices joining, leaving, moving or sleeping is dynamic change.

questions.content: A city mounts sensors on lampposts to measure pollution levels. Which IoT application is this?
questions.explanation: Measuring pollution in a city is air quality monitoring.

questions.content: A platform must manage millions of devices and handle large volumes of data. Which IoT challenge is this mainly about?
questions.explanation: Scalability is about managing very many devices and large volumes of data.

questions.content: From work, a homeowner checks on a phone whether the front door is locked. Which smart-home capability is this?
options: Monitoring and controlling devices remotely from a phone
Predicting failures of the door motor
Measuring the vibration of the door
questions.explanation: Smart-home devices such as door locks can be monitored and controlled from a phone.

questions.content: A smart blind closes automatically when a light sensor detects strong sun. Which device acts on the physical world?
options: The motor that moves the blind
questions.explanation: Actuators such as motors act on the physical world; the light sensor only senses.

questions.content: Besides translating between protocols, what else can an IoT gateway do with the data?
questions.explanation: A gateway can translate between protocols and filter or aggregate data.

questions.content: Which component of an IoT system lets people see the data and send commands?
options: The radio that sends readings to the gateway
The actuator that switches a relay
The application or user interface, such as a mobile app
questions.explanation: An application or user interface such as a mobile app or dashboard lets people see data and send commands.

questions.content: In the five-layer architecture, which layer manages business models and user privacy?
questions.explanation: The business layer on top manages the whole system, including business models and user privacy.

questions.content: What is another name for the perception layer?
questions.explanation: The perception layer is also called the sensing or device layer.

questions.content: Which IoT design goal means each device should be cheap to produce?
questions.explanation: Low cost per device is one of the design goals of IoT systems.

questions.content: A patient-monitoring device must keep working even if one network link fails. Which design goal is this?
questions.explanation: Reliability means the system keeps working correctly even when parts fail.

questions.content: A company builds protection of users' data into a product from the start instead of adding it later. Which design goal is this?
questions.explanation: Security and privacy by design build protection in from the start.

questions.content: In the home automation example described in this course, a motion sensor's event passes through the hub to which place, where a rule turns on the light?
questions.explanation: In the example, the motion sensor sends an event through a hub (gateway) to the cloud, and a rule there turns on the light. Other systems may run such rules on the hub or at the edge.

questions.content: When a rule fires, a motor opens a window. Which IoT component is the motor?
questions.explanation: Actuators change the physical world, for example by turning a motor.

questions.content: A weather station uploads its readings straight to a cloud service over its own Wi-Fi. Which communication model is this?
questions.explanation: Connecting directly to a cloud service over the internet is the device-to-cloud model.

questions.content: Which port is used for MQTT over TLS?
questions.explanation: MQTT uses port 1883 by default and 8883 over TLS.

questions.content: Which packet does an MQTT client send to show the broker it is still connected?
questions.explanation: During the keep-alive interval the client sends PINGREQ packets.

questions.content: How many steps does the MQTT QoS 2 handshake use?
questions.explanation: QoS 2 uses PUBLISH, PUBREC, PUBREL and PUBCOMP.

questions.content: What is CoAP's default port?
questions.explanation: CoAP runs over UDP, by default on port 5683.

questions.content: Which CoAP message type indicates that a received message could not be processed?
questions.explanation: A Reset (RST) message indicates that a received message could not be processed.

questions.content: Which MQTT subscription is NOT valid?
questions.explanation: The hash sign must be the last character of a topic filter.

questions.content: A CoAP client requests /humidity, but the server has no such resource. Which response code is typical?
questions.explanation: CoAP response codes are similar to HTTP: 4.04 Not Found for a missing resource.

questions.content: Why does QoS 2 create more network traffic than QoS 0?
options: It sends every message to every topic
It needs a separate TLS connection for each topic
It repeats each message until a GET arrives
It uses a four-step handshake to deliver exactly once
questions.explanation: QoS 2 delivers exactly once through a four-step handshake, at the cost of more overhead.

questions.content: How many levels does the MQTT topic factory/line1/motor3/temp have?
questions.explanation: Topic levels are separated by slashes: factory, line1, motor3 and temp.

questions.content: A CoAP client wants to change the value of an existing resource on a server. Which method fits best?
questions.explanation: Like HTTP, CoAP uses PUT to update a resource; GET reads it and DELETE removes it.

questions.content: What is the physical quantity that a sensor measures called?
questions.explanation: A sensor detects a physical quantity, called the measurand, and converts it into a signal.

questions.content: What kind of output does a digital sensor give?
options: A continuous voltage that an ADC must sample
A change in resistance that needs a current
A small voltage generated from heat
A digital value, for example over a serial bus
questions.explanation: An analog sensor gives a continuous signal; a digital sensor already gives a digital value.

questions.content: What happens to the resistance of an NTC thermistor as the temperature rises?
questions.explanation: An NTC thermistor's resistance falls as the temperature rises.

questions.content: What is the range of a sensor?
options: The smallest change in input that it can detect
The span between the smallest and largest value it can measure
The change in output per unit change in input
The time it needs to reach its final output
questions.explanation: Range is the span between the smallest and largest measurable value.

questions.content: What is a slow change in a sensor's output for the same input over time called?
questions.explanation: Stability is giving the same output over time; a slow change is called drift.

questions.content: An infrared thermometer measures a person's forehead from 5 cm away. How is it classified?
questions.explanation: It measures without touching the object, so it is a non-contact sensor.

questions.content: An IC temperature sensor outputs 10 mV per degC and 0 V at 0 degC. What is its output at 25 degC?
questions.explanation: The output is linear: 25 degC x 10 mV per degC = 250 mV.

questions.content: A datasheet says the output deviates at most 0.5 degC from the best straight line. What does this figure describe?
questions.explanation: The largest deviation from the straight line is the non-linearity error.

questions.content: A scale shows no change for loads below 2 g but responds to heavier loads. Which characteristic is the 2 g?
questions.explanation: Threshold is the smallest input, starting from zero, that produces a detectable output.

questions.content: An inductive sensor cannot detect plastic bottles on a conveyor. Which proximity sensor type could detect them?
questions.explanation: Inductive sensors detect only metal; capacitive sensors detect a change in capacitance from other objects.

questions.content: For a resistive sensor, what does the front end of a readout chain usually do?
options: Passes an excitation current and turns the resistance change into a voltage
Converts the digital codes back into an analog voltage
Stores the readings in the cloud for later analysis
Rounds every sample to the nearest ADC level
questions.explanation: The front end turns the sensor change into a voltage, for example by passing an excitation current.

questions.content: Which block of a readout chain finally processes the digital codes?
questions.explanation: The microcontroller processes the codes produced by the ADC.

questions.content: What is the sampling rate of an ADC?
options: The number of bits in each code
The size of one quantization step
The number of samples taken per second
The largest voltage it can convert
questions.explanation: The sampling rate is the number of samples per second.

questions.content: What does quantization turn a continuous input into?
questions.explanation: Quantization maps each value to the nearest discrete level, so the input becomes a staircase.

questions.content: Why is the sampling rate usually not set much higher than needed?
questions.explanation: A sampling rate far above what is needed wastes power and produces more data.

questions.content: How many output codes does a 16-bit ADC have?
questions.explanation: An N-bit ADC has 2^N codes; 2^16 = 65536.

questions.content: An application needs 0.5 degC resolution from a 10 mV per degC sensor. What is the largest acceptable LSB?
questions.explanation: The LSB in degC must be at most 0.5 degC: 0.5 degC x 10 mV per degC = 5 mV.

questions.content: A sensor already gives 0 to 2 V and the ADC's full scale is 2.048 V. Is extra gain useful?
options: Yes; a gain of about 40 is needed
Yes; the ADC cannot read signals above 1 V
No; the ADC needs a signal of at least 5 V
Hardly; the signal already uses most of the ADC range
questions.explanation: The signal already comes close to full scale, so more gain would risk saturation without much benefit.

questions.content: A strain gauge changes its resistance, not its voltage. What must the readout do first?
options: Turn the resistance change into a voltage, for example with an excitation current
Send the resistance value directly to the microcontroller
Lower the sampling rate below the signal frequency
Remove the ADC and use a digital sensor instead
questions.explanation: The front end must turn the resistance change into a voltage before amplification and conversion.

questions.content: How does quantization error usually behave in a measurement?
options: Like a change of sampling rate
questions.explanation: With rounding to the nearest level, quantization error behaves like a small added noise.

questions.content: What output resistance does an ideal opamp have?
questions.explanation: An ideal opamp has zero output resistance and infinite input resistance.

questions.content: A designer is choosing an opamp for a thermocouple amplifier with a gain of 500. What should be checked before buying it?
options: Only its supply voltage, because all opamps behave alike at any gain
Only its price, because non-idealities never matter in sensor readout
Only its output current, because the input side does not affect accuracy
Its datasheet limits, such as offset, against the needs of the sensor and application
questions.explanation: Designers check the opamp's datasheet limits against the sensor and application; with a gain of 500 and microvolt signals, offset and other non-idealities matter.

questions.content: What is a typical size of an opamp's input offset voltage?
questions.explanation: Input offset voltage is typically microvolts to a few millivolts.

questions.content: Which kind of opamp inputs gives a very high input resistance?
questions.explanation: Opamps with CMOS or FET inputs have a very high input resistance.

questions.content: In which situation do opamp non-idealities matter most?
options: When the signal is large and slow
When the gain is exactly 1 and the source resistance is low
When the sensor signal is tiny
questions.explanation: Errors matter most with tiny signals, large gain, high source resistance or fast signals.

questions.content: An amplifier with a gain of 10 uses an opamp with a 2 mV input offset. What output error does the offset cause?
questions.explanation: The offset is multiplied by the gain: 2 mV x 10 = 20 mV.

questions.content: Raising an amplifier's gain from 10 to 100 with the same opamp changes its bandwidth how?
options: It becomes about ten times lower
It becomes about ten times higher
questions.explanation: The gain-bandwidth product is roughly constant, so ten times more gain gives about ten times less bandwidth.

questions.content: An opamp on a 5 V supply is asked to output 7 V. What happens?
options: The output reaches 7 V but slowly
The output saturates near the supply voltage
The opamp adds an offset of 2 V
questions.explanation: The output cannot swing beyond the supply voltages, so it saturates.

questions.content: A sensor with Rs = 2 kOhm feeds an amplifier with Rin = 2 kOhm. What fraction of the sensor voltage does the amplifier see?
An opamp has a slew rate of 1 V per microsecond. What is the shortest time its output needs to rise by 5 V?
questions.explanation: The output can change at most 1 V per microsecond, so a 5 V step needs at least 5 microseconds.
